{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts frequently use specific organizational abbreviations (BFG, EuGH) and titles (Dr., Mag., Richter) to identify entities. The main challenge is distinguishing between person names and organization names when they appear in similar contexts (e.g., 'Dr. Name' vs 'Dr. Name GmbH'). The rules prioritize context anchors like 'Richter', 'Richterin', 'vertreten durch', and specific legal body names to ensure precision.",
  "strategy": "Use specific context anchors (titles, prepositions, legal phrases) combined with capitalized name patterns to distinguish between persons and organizations, while explicitly handling common German legal abbreviations.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use capture groups ($1) for names to allow context matching without including the context in the final entity text.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "person_judge_title",
      "description": "Extracts person names following judicial titles like 'Richter', 'Richterin', 'Dr.', 'Hon.-Prof.'",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Richter(?:in)?|Dr\\.(?:in)?|Hon\\.-Prof\\.|Mag\\.?)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "High precision for judges and experts; context ensures we don't match 'Dr.' in other contexts."
    },
    {
      "name": "person_complainant",
      "description": "Extracts person names following 'Beschwerdesache' (complainant)",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "Beschwerdesache\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Directly identifies the party in the case, a common pattern in legal headers."
    },
    {
      "name": "person_representative",
      "description": "Extracts person names following 'vertreten durch' (represented by)",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:vertreten\\s+durch|durch)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Identifies legal representatives; context prevents matching organization names that might follow."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_bundesfinanzgericht",
      "description": "Matches full name and abbreviation of the Federal Financial Court",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Bundesfinanzgericht|BFG)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Core entity in tax law; handles both full name and common abbreviation."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_verwaltungsgerichtshof",
      "description": "Matches full name and abbreviation of the Administrative Court",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Verwaltungsgerichtshof|VwGh|VwGH)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Core entity for appeals; handles variations in capitalization and abbreviation."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_finanzamt_general",
      "description": "Matches Finanzamt with optional suffixes (e.g., Vorarlberg, Österreich, Braunau Ried)",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\bFinanzamt(?:\\s+(?:Vorarlberg|Österreich|Braunau Ried|Graz-Stadt))?\\b(?:es)?\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "'Finanzamt' is the most frequent entity; handles genitive case ('Finanzamtes') and specific locations."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_eu_gerichtshof",
      "description": "Matches European Court of Justice variations",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Europäische Gerichtshof|EuGH)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "\nHandles the EU court entity which appears in legal reasoning."}, 
    { 
"name":"org_law_firm","description":"Matches law firms identified by 'OG', 'GmbH', 'KG' following a name","format":"regex","pattern":"([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*\\s+(?:Stb|Steuerberatung|Treuhand)\\s+(?:OG|GmbH|KG))","output_template":{"text":"$0","start":"$start","end":"$end","type":"organisation"},"output_key":"entities","priority":"5","reasoning":"Identifies law firms which are organizations but look like names; suffixes like GmbH/OG are strong disambiguators."} 
  ], 
  "_deleted_rules_":[""] 
}

        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"

      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "The previous rule missed specific long-form names like 'Finanzamt Freistadt Rohrbach Urfahr' and 'Finanzamt für Großbetriebe'. This pattern explicitly includes these known suffixes."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_verwaltungsgerichtshof",
      "description": "Matches full name and abbreviation of the Administrative Court, including genitive forms.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Verwaltungsgerichtshof(?:es)?|VwGh|VwGH)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "The previous rule missed 'Verwaltungsgerichtshofes' (genitive). This pattern includes the optional 'es' suffix to catch all forms."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_eu_gerichtshof",
      "description": "Matches European Court of Justice variations including 'Europäischen' and 'Europäische'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Europäische(?:n)?\\s+Gerichtshof|EuGH)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "The previous rule missed 'Europäischen Gerichtshofs' (genitive). This pattern handles the adjective variation."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_law_firm",
      "description": "Matches law firms identified by 'OG', 'GmbH', 'KG' following a name, ensuring the preceding word is a name part.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*\\s+(?:Stb|Steuerberatung|Treuhand|Rechtsanwalts-?\\s+Kommandit-Partnerschaft)\\s+(?:OG|GmbH|KG))",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "The previous rule was too broad and missed complex firm names like 'Rechtsanwalts- Kommandit-Partnerschaft'. This pattern explicitly includes that variation."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_pensionsversicherung",
      "description": "Matches Pensionsversicherungsanstalt and similar social security organizations.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Pensionsversicherungsanstalt|SVB|Sozialversicherung)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 4,
      "reasoning": "The training data shows 'PENSIONSVERSICHERUNGSANSTALT' as an organization. This rule adds it to the list of recognized entities."
    },
    {
      "name": "org_magistrat",
      "description": "Matches Magistrat and its variations (e.g., Magistrat der Stadt Wien).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Magistrat(?:(?:\\s+der\\s+Stadt\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)?(?:\\s+Abteilung\\s+\\d+)?)?)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "The training data shows 'Magistrat der Stadt Wien' and 'Magistratsabteilung 67'. This rule captures the full context."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

IMPORTANT:
- Do NOT assume entities are capitalized; check the training data.
- Prefer structural patterns (\d+, [A-Z][a-z]+) over memorized alternations.
- When multiple entity types share similar text, use surrounding context to disambiguate.

- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:

- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:

- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

IMPORTANT:
- Do NOT assume entities are capitalized; check the training data.
- Prefer structural patterns (\d+, [A-Z][a-z]+) over memorized alternations.
- When multiple entity types share similar text, use surrounding context to disambiguate.
